query: I'm new to investing and have student loans. What should I prioritize first with my savings?

recommendations.title: Complete Emergency Fund Before Increasing Investment Activity
recommendations.summary: Prioritize building your 6-month emergency fund ($22,000) in a high-yield savings account before making new investments, given your lack of emergency savings and moderate debt load.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: With no emergency fund, moderate debt ($38,000), and conservative risk tolerance (loss comfort 3/10), your first priority should be financial stability. Your current $15,000 cash position represents 60% of assets but falls short of your $22,000 emergency fund goal. Given monthly expenses of $3,800, you need approximately $7,000 more to reach 6 months of coverage. As a beginner investor with student loans and negative net worth (-$13,000), building this safety net protects you from forced liquidation of investments during emergencies and prevents accumulating high-interest debt. Your current holdings in VTTSX (target-date fund) and BND (bonds) are appropriate for your conservative profile and should be maintained but not expanded until emergency savings are complete.
recommendations.suggested_action: Direct all available savings toward a high-yield savings account (currently offering 4-5% APY) until emergency fund reaches $22,000. Maintain current investment holdings without additional contributions.

recommendations.title: Maintain Current Conservative Investment Mix
recommendations.summary: Keep existing VTTSX and BND holdings unchanged while focusing savings elsewhere, as this allocation appropriately matches your conservative risk profile and beginner experience level.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: Your current 40% investment allocation split between VTTSX (Vanguard Target Retirement fund) and BND (Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF) demonstrates appropriate diversification for a conservative investor. VTTSX provides automatic rebalancing and age-appropriate asset allocation, while BND adds bond stability. This mix aligns well with your risk tolerance, beginner experience, and medium-term horizon. However, with negative net worth and no emergency fund, maintaining (not growing) this position is prudent. These holdings provide modest growth potential while you address foundational financial priorities. Avoid selling these assets unless facing true emergency, as you'd lose compound growth benefits and potentially incur taxes or penalties.
recommendations.suggested_action: Hold all current positions. Do not make additional contributions until emergency fund is complete. Continue any employer 401(k) match if available, but redirect other savings to emergency fund.

recommendations.title: Develop Student Loan Paydown Strategy
recommendations.summary: Create a systematic approach to reducing your moderate debt load, focusing on high-interest loans first while maintaining minimum payments on all obligations.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: With $38,000 in liabilities (likely student loans given your profile) and income of $72,000, your debt-to-income ratio is approximately 53%, which is moderate but significant. After covering monthly expenses ($3,800) and taxes (estimated $1,100/month), you have roughly $900-1,000 monthly for savings and debt paydown. Given current student loan interest rates (5-8% for federal, potentially higher for private), high-interest debt likely costs more than investment returns. After completing your emergency fund, prioritize extra payments toward loans exceeding 6% interest while maintaining minimums on lower-rate debt. This reduces financial risk, improves cash flow, and psychologically prepares you for larger investments. The avalanche method (highest interest first) will save the most money long-term.
recommendations.suggested_action: List all debts with interest rates. After emergency fund completion, allocate 50-60% of surplus income toward highest-rate debt while building remaining toward house down payment goal.

recommendations.title: Future Phase: Add I Bonds for House Down Payment Savings
recommendations.summary: Once emergency fund is complete (12+ months from now), consider Series I Savings Bonds for tax-advantaged, inflation-protected savings toward your 5-7 year house down payment goal.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: After establishing emergency savings, your medium-priority goal of accumulating $60,000 for a house down payment in 5-7 years needs a dedicated vehicle. Series I Savings Bonds offer inflation protection, tax deferral, and potential tax-free use for qualified purposes, with current rates around 5%. The 1-year lockup period and 3-month interest penalty before 5 years align with your medium liquidity needs and medium-term horizon. You can purchase up to $10,000 annually per person ($15,000 including tax refund purchases), allowing systematic accumulation. This complements your existing conservative holdings while providing government-backed security appropriate for a major life goal. This is a future recommendation—implement only after emergency fund completion and while managing debt obligations.
recommendations.suggested_action: Phase 2 action (12-18 months out): Begin annual $10,000 I Bond purchases, creating a ladder for house down payment. Maintain flexibility by staggering purchases quarterly.
